To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
octopaminergic modulatory influences on visual information processing in the fly's brain are state-dependent and that the modulation is similar in the different states.

(1) the response properties of the V1 motion sensitive neuron in the fly are modulated by the octopamine neuromodulator; (2) these changes are similar to the effects of locomotor activity; (3) the modulation of the response characteristics by octopamine does not significantly alter the processing of naturalistically generated optic flow.
the octopaminergic neuromodulation of the V1 cell does not alter the processing of natural optic flow.
In summary, our research is concerned with
how visual information is processed by the brain and how it affects the behavior of an animal.
the role of octopaminergic neuromodulation in the visual system of flies.
the role of neuromodulatory substances in the control of neuronal processing of sensory information in the fly.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
octopamine does not alter the processing of optic-flow in a way that would support the control of the fly's flight behaviour.

octopamine does not alter the processing of natural optic flow, but rather increases the gain of responses to optic flow, which is in line with a proposed role in the enhancement of motion detection in general.
the modulation of V1 responses by octopamine is not sufficient for a specific function in the control of flight.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

octopaminergic neuromodulation of the fly V1 neuron enhances the response to naturalistic optic flow by increasing spike rates and decreasing latencies, but does not change the neuronal tuning properties.
octopamine modulates the V1 response properties in such a way that the processing of optic information is optimized for the specific conditions of flight.

octopaminergic neuromodulation of the fly visual system is not only important to adjust the response dynamics to the range of velocities encountered during flight, but also to enhance the neuronal responses during sustained stimulation with naturalistic image sequences.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the state-dependent modulation of visual information processing by octopamine in the fly's brain might not be primarily geared to the detection of optic flow cues, but to other aspects of the visual input.

the modulation of motion-sensitive neurons is likely to have a strong impact on the temporal dynamics of the neuronal response, but does not seem to alter the overall response characteristics in a way that would affect the processing of natural visual stimuli.
the processing of complex naturalistic stimuli is not necessarily affected by neuromodulation.
